آخر الأخبار التحليلات المغرب العربي شؤون أفريقية الإسلام السياسي اليمن العراق ليبيا اقتصاد أسواق المال عملات رقمية تكنولوجيا سياحة وسفر سيارات الذكاء الاصطناعي الطاقة المتجددة مساحة خضراء الرأي منوعات 2026/10/21 07:31 م وضع ليلي تابعونا على السوشيال ميديا سياسة «وجوه غريبة».. ذريعة الجيش السوداني والإخوان لقتل المدنيين (خاص) العين الإخبارية- خاص الأربعاء 2026/10/21 06:59 م بتوقيت أبوظبي عبدالفتاح البرهان قائد الجيش السوداني تم تحديثه الأربعاء 2026/10/21 07:27 م بتوقيت أبوظبي "الوجوه الغريبة" تعبير يستخدمه الجيش السوداني وكتائب الإخوان كذريعة لقتل مئات المدنيين في الأيام الأخيرة، وفق خبير. وتصاعدت الهجمات على الأسواق والمناطق المأهولة بالسكان في كردفان (جنوب) ودارفور (غرب)، والتي أسفرت عن سقوط مئات القتلى والجرحى. إدانة حقوقية وأدانت 3 منظمات حقوقية سودانية ودولية تصاعد الهجمات الجوية والمدفعية المكثفة التي قالت إن "الجيش السوداني يشنها بالتنسيق الميداني المباشر مع الكتائب والميليشيات العسكرية التابعة لتنظيم الإخوان، التي أسفرت عن سقوط مئات القتلى والجرحى في أوساط المدنيين بفضائح إنسانية متتالية في مناطق غرب كردفان وجنوب دارفور". وأفادت المنظمة السودانية لحقوق الإنسان "شرا"، ومنظمة "قادم" لتمكين اللاجئين، والمنظمة الأفريقية للحقوق والتنمية "أفورد"، في بيان مشترك، بأن "الغارات الجوية والهجمات بالطائرات المُسيّرة استهدفت بشكل مباشر تجمعات المدنيين والأسواق المكتظة". وأشارت إلى استهداف حافلة نقل تجارية تقل نساء وأطفالا وطلابا في محلية الدبب بغرب كردفان، ما أدى إلى سقوط أكثر من 300 قتيل وجريح، إلى جانب القصف الدموي على سوق مدينة المجلد وسوق المواشي في نيالا الذي خلف نحو 130 قتيلا وجريحا، إضافة إلى الاستهداف المتكرر لأسواق النهود وأبو زبد. وأضافت: "تعد كتائب الإخوان المسلمين المسلحة وفي مقدمتها ميليشيات البراء بن مالك وأذرع الحركة الإسلامية شريكا فعليا وميدانيا في التخطيط والتنفيذ لهذه الهجمات العشوائية التي تستهدف الأعيان المدنية والمناطق المأهولة بالسكان، عبر الاستمرار في تجييش الصراع وإجهاض مساعي التهدئة لحساب أجندات حزبية ضيقة". وطالبت المنظمات الحقوقية الأمم المتحدة ومجلس حقوق الإنسان والاتحاد الأفريقي بفتح تحقيقات دولية مستقلة وشفافة لملاحقة قيادات الجيش وحلفائهم، ومحاسبة كافة المتورطين في ارتكاب جرائم الحرب والانتهاكات الصارخة للقانون الدولي الإنساني. وجوه غريبة من جانبه، قال النجمي عثمان، المحلل السياسي السوداني، لـ"العين الإخبارية": "منذ أن أشعل جيش الحركة الإسلامية والإخوان الحرب في السودان في 15 أبريل/نيسان 2023، ظل الجيش يستهدف المواطنين بصورة مباشرة، وكان يصفهم بأنهم حواضن الدعم السريع، كما أطلق عليهم وصف الوجوه الغريبة". وأضاف: "كل شخص لا ينتمي إلى هذه الجماعة، أو لا يدعمها إعلاميا أو عسكريا، أو لا يستنفر لصالحها، يعد في نظرها من الوجوه الغريبة، ولا سيما الأشخاص القادمين من غرب السودان، وتحديدا دارفور وكردفان". وتابع: "ظل الجيش يرتكب هذه الانتهاكات، بدءًا من ولاية الجزيرة (وسط)، مرورا بالخرطوم، وتحديدا منطقة مايو وجنوب الحزام، وصولا إلى الحاج يوسف". وقال: "يقصف الطيران الحربي والطائرات المسيّرة المدنيين الأبرياء، فيما تتولى قوات على الأرض، بينها كتائب البراء وغيرها من الحركات التي وصفها بحركات الارتزاق، عمليات الذبح والتنكيل". وأوضح أن "آخر هذه الانتهاكات كان ما حدث في مدينة الدبيبات، وكذلك مدينة الضعين، وسوق المواشي في نيالا، وسوق النعام في جنوب كردفان". وقال: "خلال هذا الأسبوع، وصل رصد أعداد القتلى المدنيين إلى 1340 شخصا، من الأطفال والنساء وكبار السن والرجال وغيرهم، في الأسواق التي استُهدفت في كردفان وجنوب كردفان وشمال كردفان، بما في ذلك أبو زبد ونيالا والضعين". جرائم متواصلة وأكد أنه "في مدينة سودري بشمال كردفان، دخلت حركات الارتزاق، كان الطيران يضرب من الجو، فيما كانت تلك الحركات تذبح المواطنين على الأرض. دخل أفراد منها منازل المواطنين، وصوّروا أنفسهم داخلها، وتحدوا النساء المقيمات فيها، مطالبين إياهن بالعودة إلى منطقة سودري، ووجهوا إليهن تحديا مباشرا وتهديدا، قائلين لهن حرفيا: "تعالين إلى بيوتكن إن استطعتن". وأعرب عن اعتقاده بأن إدانة المنظمات الحقوقية لهذه الممارسات تمثل خطوة نحو تصنيف جرائم الجيش والإخوان، لكنها ليست كافية، مطالبا بأن "يضطلع المجتمع الدولي بمهامه ومسؤولياته، وأن يعاقب المسؤولين عن هذه الجرائم، على غرار العقوبات الأمريكية المفروضة على قادة الجيش والحركة الإسلامية، وأن يتدخل مجلس الأمن، حتى بموجب الفصل السابع، من أجل حماية المدنيين". وقال: "أرى أن التعامل مع هذا الجيش يجب أن يستند إلى أدوات القوة والعقوبات، ولا سيما من خلال مجلس الأمن والأمم المتحدة وغيرها من الجهات الدولية، بما يتيح كبح جماح هذا الجيش". وختم بالقول: "أطالب المجتمع الدولي بالاضطلاع بمسؤولياته ومحاسبة الدواعش، حتى لا يستمر القتل والمذابح. فقد تجاوز عدد القتلى خلال هذا الأسبوع 1300 شخص، وقد يصل العدد إلى 1500، في ظل وجود مفقودين وأشخاص لم تُعرف هوياتهم". السودان غرفة الأخبار #تقارير_خاصة السوداني محي الدين سالم خلال اجتماع وزراء خارجية الكوميسا في هراري هراري 21 أكتوبر 2026 – طالب وزير الخارجية السوداني محي الدين سالم، الأربعاء، بتشكيل آلية أفريقية موحدة لمواجهة المليشيات المتمردة والجماعات الإرهابية. وشارك سالم، مترئسًا وفد السودان، في أعمال الاجتماع الـ21 لوزراء خارجية دول السوق المشتركة للشرق والجنوب الأفريقي “الكوميسا”، المنعقد في العاصمة الزيمبابوية هراري. ودعا محي الدين سالم، خلال حديثه في الاجتماع، إلى تشكيل “آلية إقليمية موحدة للتعامل مع التحديات الأمنية والسياسية، ومواجهة الحركات المتمردة والجماعات الإرهابية العابرة للحدود التي تستغل الأزمات لتهريب السلع والإضرار بالاستقرار الاقتصادي ورفع تكاليف المعيشة”. وطالب بضرورة تكامل جهود دول المنطقة لمكافحة الجريمة المنظمة والاتجار بالمخدرات، والتصدي للمخاطر التي تهدد المجتمعات الأفريقية، خاصة النساء والشباب وكبار السن، في ظل استغلال أوضاع الفقر والهشاشة. وأشار إلى أن استقرار دول المنطقة يمثل شرطًا أساسيًا لنجاح جهود التكامل الاقتصادي، وتعزيز التجارة البينية، وتحقيق الأمن الغذائي، وحماية الحدود. وحث دول الكوميسا على توحيد الرؤى والمواقف إزاء التهديدات المشتركة، بما يعزز قدرة القارة على معالجة أزماتها وتحقيق الاستقرار المستدام. وقال الوزير بحسب بيان لوزارة الخارجية إن موقف السودان ثابت حيال توصيف قوات الدعم السريع بأنها «مليشيا متمردة» في الأدبيات والمداولات الإقليمية، نظرًا إلى الجرائم والانتهاكات الجسيمة التي ارتكبتها بحق المدنيين، إضافة إلى ما وصفه بالدمار الممنهج للبنية التحتية. ودعا وزراء خارجية دول الكوميسا إلى زيارة العاصمة الخرطوم للوقوف ميدانيًا على حجم الدمار والآثار التي خلفتها اعتداءات قوات الدعم السريع على البلاد ومؤسساتها. ويخوض الجيش السوداني، منذ 15 أبريل 2023، حربًا ضد قوات الدعم السريع، اندلعت في الخرطوم، قبل أن تنحصر بصورة رئيسية في إقليمي كردفان والنيل الأزرق، فيما لا يزال معظم إقليم دارفور تحت سيطرة قوات الدعم السريع. وقالت وزارة الخارجية، في بيان، إن اجتماع الكوميسا أجاز التوصيات الواردة في تقرير حالة السلم والأمن في السودان والمنطقة. وأفادت بأن التوصيات شملت احترام سيادة السودان ووحدة أراضيه واستقلال مؤسساته الوطنية، علاوة على الرفض التام للتدخلات الخارجية والإمدادات العسكرية والمالية للأطراف المسلحة والمليشيات. ودعت التوصيات، بحسب البيان، إلى تنسيق جهود الكوميسا والاتحاد الأفريقي والمبادرات الأفريقية الداعمة للسلام، وتجنب تعارض المسارات التفاوضية. وأوضحت الوزارة أن التوصيات تضمنت دعم الترتيبات الفنية واللوجستية لإعادة افتتاح المقر الدائم لمحكمة العدل التابعة للكوميسا في الخرطوم، إلى جانب حشد المؤسسات التنموية والقطاع الخاص الأفريقي للمساهمة في جهود التعافي وإعادة الإعمار في السودان. الكلمات: إعادة الإعمار في السودان الكوميسا قوات الدعم السريع محي الدين سالم وزارة الخارجية السودانية مقالات ذات صلة «المنصوري» يؤدي اليمين وزيرًا للثروة الأربعاء، أعمال اجتماع تنسيقي موسع برعاية الأمم المتحدة لبحث سبل تفعيل مبادرات السلام في السودان. ويشهد الاجتماع مشاركة واسعة من ممثلي 26 دولة ومنظمة دولية، في محاولة لكسر الجمود السياسي الحالي رغم غياب أطراف النزاع المباشرة عن طاولة الحوار. يضم الاجتماع، الذي يعد السادس من نوعه ضمن سلسلة اللقاءات التنسيقية، أعضاء مجموعة الرباعية التي تشمل الولايات المتحدة ومصر والسعودية والإمارات. كما يشارك فيه الأعضاء الدائمون في مجلس الأمن الدولي، إلى جانب مسؤولين رفيعي المستوى من دول الجوار السوداني، لا سيما إثيوبيا وتشاد، لضمان رؤية إقليمية شاملة للحل. تهدف المشاورات الجارية في قصر الأمم إلى توحيد الجهود الدولية وتنسيق مبادرات الوساطة المتعددة لتجنب تضارب المسارات. ويسعى المشاركون إلى الدفع باتجاه تهدئة شاملة تمهد الطريق للتوصل إلى حل سياسي تفاوضي ينهي الأزمة التي تعصف بالبلاد منذ أكثر من عام ونصف. يركز المجتمعون على بحث الأبعاد الإقليمية المعقدة للنزاع السوداني وتداعياته على الأمن والسلم في القارة الأفريقية. ومن المقرر أن يصدر عن الدول المشاركة بيان مشترك في ختام المداولات، يحدد خارطة طريق للتحرك الدولي المقبل والضغط على الأطراف المتصارعة للعودة إلى المسار السلمي. شدد المبعوث الخاص للأمين العام للأمم المتحدة إلى السودان، بيكا هافيستو، في افتتاح الجلسات على ضرورة تحويل النوايا الدولية إلى خطوات عملية على الأرض. وأشار هافيستو إلى أن قيمة هذا اللقاء تكمن في القدرة على ترجمة الشعور بضرورة التحرك العاجل إلى أفعال ملموسة تنهي معاناة الشعب السوداني. حذر المبعوث الأممي من استمرار النزاع مع اقتراب دخوله العام الرابع بحلول أبريل 2027، مؤكداً على ضرورة بذل أقصى الجهود الممكنة لوقف نزيف الدماء. ودعا إلى أن تكون هذه المحطة الدولية بداية حقيقية لمسار السلام، بدلاً من أن تكون مجرد علامة زمنية لعام إضافي من الحرب والدمار. من جهته، أكد سكرتير الدولة السويسري بوزارة الشؤون الخارجية، ألكسندر فازل أن حماية المدنيين يجب أن تظل الأولوية القصوى للمجتمع الدولي في الوقت الراهن. وأوضح فازل أنه لا يمكن رهن حماية الأبرياء بالتوصل إلى وقف كامل لإطلاق النار، بل يجب التحرك فوراً لضمان سلامتهم وتأمين احتياجاتهم الأساسية. أشار المسؤول السويسري إلى ضرورة ضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية دون عوائق إلى المناطق المتضررة من القتال. وشدد على أن الوضع الإنساني المتدهور يتطلب استجابة دولية عاجلة تتجاوز التعقيدات السياسية والعسكرية القائمة بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع. تأتي هذه التحركات الدبلوماسية في وقت تشير فيه تقارير العاملين في المجال الإنساني إلى سقوط أكثر من 200 ألف قتيل منذ اندلاع المواجهات في أبريل 2023. وقد تسببت الحرب في تفشي المجاعة في عدة مناطق، بالإضافة إلى موجات نزوح واسعة النطاق داخلياً وخارجياً، مما خلق واحدة من أسوأ الأزمات الإنسانية في العالم. تصاعدت وتيرة العمليات العسكرية مؤخراً مع الاعتماد المتزايد على الطائرات المسيرة في ولايتي كردفان والنيل الأزرق. وأفادت مصادر أممية بأن موحد". جاء ذلك خلال الاجتماع التشاوري حول تعزيز تنسيق مبادرات وجهود السلام في السودان، الذي عقد اليوم الأربعاء في مقر الأمم المتحدة بجنيف، بمشاركة ممثلين رفيعي المستوى من 22 دولة، إلى جانب الأمم المتحدة، والاتحاد الأفريقي، والاتحاد الأوروبي، والهيئة الحكومية الدولية المعنية بالتنمية (إيغاد)، وجامعة الدول العربية. يعد هذا الاجتماع السادس من نوعه، ويشكل آلية تنسيقية هامة تجمع الأطراف الدولية والإقليمية المشاركة في جهود حل النزاع في السودان، ولا يضم في مداولاته الحكومة السودانية أو قوات الدعم السريع، رغم أنه يتم التشاور مع أطراف النزاع قبل انعقاده واطلاعهم على نتائجه بعد اختتامه. وقد عقدت الاجتماعات السابقة في القاهرة، وجيبوتي، ونواكشوط، وبروكسل. وفي كلمته الافتتاحية، أكد هافيستو أن أصوات الشعب السوداني يجب أن توجه المداولات، وأن "تطلعاتهم يجب أن تظل المعيار الذي نقيس به مدى تقدمنا". وأوضح أن المناقشات ستتمحور حول جهود خفض التصعيد وبناء الثقة بين الأطراف، ومسار الانتقال نحو مرحلة سياسية انتقالية وعملية سياسية يقودها السودانيون، بالإضافة إلى الأبعاد الإقليمية للنزاع وكيفية منع تدهور الأوضاع وامتداد النزاع بشكل أكبر إلى الدول المجاورة. وأشار هافيستو إلى أن قيمة هذا الاجتماع تعتمد على قدرة المشاركين على تحويل الإدراك المشترك لمدى ضرورة التحرك العاجل إلى إجراءات عملية، قائلا: "نحن مدينون للشعب السوداني باهتمام مستمر، وانخراط متسق، وعمل حازم. ومع اقتراب شهر نيسان/أبريل 2027، يجب علينا بذل كل ما في وسعنا لضمان أن يشكل هذا التاريخ نقطة تحول نحو السلام، بدلا من أن يكون بداية لعام آخر من الحرب والمعاناة. إن هدفنا من هذا الاجتماع هو تسخير جهودنا الجماعية لخدمة الشعب السوداني". لا أحد بمنأى عن التبعات من جانبه، قال ألكسندر فاسيل، وزير الدولة السويسري للشؤون الخارجية، إنه بعد مرور 1285 يوما على الحرب في السودان، أصبحت اليوم "بالغة التعقيد وأكثر فتكا بكثير"، حيث تشهد البلاد واحدة من أسوأ الأزمات الإنسانية وأزمات الحماية في العالم. وأكد فاسيل أن سويسرا، التي شاركت في استضافة Convened in late 1996 under IGAD’s newly established conflict-resolution mandate, the talks culminated on 3 January 1997 in the creation of a 41-member National Salvation Council, with representation allocated to the four major clan families and smaller communities. Although Sodere did not produce a lasting government, it established a broad-based framework for political representation that subsequent reconciliation efforts would revisit The collapse of the Somali state in January 1991 left political authority dispersed among armed factions, while successive international efforts failed to establish a national government capable of consolidating control. The Addis Ababa Agreement of 1993 brought leading factions into a common framework, but agreement on paper did not resolve the struggle for power in Mogadishu; by the time the last United Nations troops withdrew in March 1995, the underlying competition remained intact. Rivalry between Ali Mahdi Mohamed and the Aideed camp, which passed to Hussein Aideed following General Mohamed Farah Aideed’s death in August 1996, continued to obstruct the emergence of a national political authority. The consequences extended beyond the capital. In the border region of Gedo, Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI) established a presence centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometers from Ethiopia, which Addis Ababa regarded as a base for a movement responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linked to other armed groups opposed to its government. Somalia’s fragmentation thus presented Ethiopia with a problem that international mediation alone had not resolved, the absence of a functioning state was not merely prolonging conflict within Somalia but also leaving neighboring territory exposed to armed networks that could operate across the border. This gave Ethiopia a direct security interest in the restoration of Somali political authority. The expansion of regional institutions in 1996 provided an important foundation for a more coordinated response to Somalia’s political fragmentation, creating a framework through which Ethiopia could address its security concerns while contributing to a regional effort to restore Somali political dialogue. Founded in 1986 as the Intergovernmental Authority on Drought and Development, with a mandate centred on drought and desertification, the organization was reconstituted as the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) following the amendment of its founding instrument in Nairobi on 21 March 1996 and its relaunch at the Djibouti summit of 25–26 November. The revised charter incorporated the prevention, management and resolution of inter-state and intra-state conflicts through dialogue, placing peace and security alongside food security and economic cooperation among the organization’s priorities. This change reflected a broader recognition that the conflicts confronting the Horn of Africa required regional mechanisms capable of addressing their political and security dimensions. For Ethiopia, whose border security was directly affected by the absence of effective authority in Somalia, IGAD’s expanded mandate offered a legitimate avenue for supporting reconciliation through regional diplomacy. The framework connected Ethiopia’s immediate security concerns with the wider regional interest in reducing conflict and restoring political order in Somalia, giving its diplomatic engagement an institutional foundation and a shared regional purpose. Although divisions among IGAD members, including the severance of relations with Sudan by Ethiopia, Eritrea and Uganda during the preceding year, complicated regional cooperation, the organization’s expanded mandate established an important basis for renewed engagement. OAU strengthened this framework in July 1996, when its Yaoundé resolution recognized Meles Zenawi, then outgoing OAU chairman, as holding a special mandate to facilitate peace in Somalia and supported efforts by IGAD member states to reactivate their initiatives. This endorsement connected the emerging regional effort to the OAU’s broader diplomatic role and reinforced the legitimacy of renewed attempts to bring Somali factions into negotiations. Ethiopia subsequently informed the United Nations Security Council that it had convened the Sodere conference in November 1996 in accordance with an IGAD mandate. Operating within this reinforced regional framework, Ethiopian conduct in the second half of 1996 ran along two tracks that differed in instrument yet converged through local partnerships. On the military track, Ethiopia acted against Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI), an Islamist group that had established a presence in the Gedo region centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometres from the Ethiopian border. Addis Ababa regarded AIAI as a direct security threat, holding it responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linking it to other armed networks opposed to the Ethiopian government. Ethiopian forces therefore crossed into Gedo on 9 August 1996 to attack AIAI bases, and fighting continued through December. The fourth major assault on the group, launched on 11 June 1997, captured Luuq and Buulo Haawo and deprived AIAI of its last major bases in the region. This military campaign ran in parallel with a political initiative that sought to harness Somali opposition to AIAI and embed Ethiopia’s border-security objectives within a broader reconciliation process. On the political track, Ethiopia convened Somali leaders at the Sodere resort for roughly six weeks of talks, which ended on 3 January 1997 with a declaration signed by 27 leaders representing 26 factions. The declaration created a National Salvation Council of 41 members and a National Executive Committee of 11 members led by five co-chairmen, with authority to speak for the Council and to prepare a Transitional Central Authority or Provisional Central Government, and it committed the signatories to a National Reconciliation Conference at Bossaso. The Somali National Front, a competitor of AIAI for control of Gedo, was among the signatories. That overlap offered Somali opponents of AIAI an institutional route to national standing and tied a border security objective to a political process that Somali actors could own. The composition of the Council contains the process’s most durable contribution. Nine seats went to each of the four major clan families, Darod, Hawiye, Rahanweyn and Dir, and five to smaller groups, a distribution that totals 41 and approximates the half-share later formalized for minorities under the 4.5 formula. For the first time the Darod accepted parity among the main clan families. That principle of clan-family parity, first given institutional expression at Sodere, was subsequently formalized at the Arta conference in 2000 and then applied at scale by the Mbagathi process, which in 2004 allocated 61 seats to each of the four major families and 31 to the minority bloc within a 275-member Transitional Federal Parliament. By converting a contest over who speaks for Somalia into a bounded negotiation over who sits within each family’s allotment, parity supplied the mechanism through which Sodere moved Somali politics from open military competition toward transitional institutions. Sodere’s significance extended beyond the representational framework it helped establish to the regional diplomacy through which that framework was pursued. Ethiopia’s subsequent involvement in Somali reconciliation formed part of a recurring pattern that included hosting the 1993 Addis Ababa conference, convening Sodere in 1996 and 1997, participating in the IGAD-mediated Mbagathi talks that produced the Transitional Federal Charter in 2004, and contributing troops to the African Union missions in Somalia, AMISOM and ATMIS, and now AUSSOM. The Mbagathi record offers particularly clear evidence that Somali actors themselves regarded Ethiopia’s participation as consequential. In February 2004, six faction leaders of the Somali Restoration and Reconstruction Council announced that they would stay out of the final phase of the talks while Ethiopia was absent from the table. Hussein Aideed, who had succeeded his father General Mohamed Farah Aideed in 1996 and had remained outside the Sodere process the following year, now argued that a regional peace process required consensus among neighbouring states as well as among Somalis. His position marked a shift from contesting Ethiopia’s involvement in 1997 to treating the participation of neighboring states as a condition of a credible settlement, illustrating how the regional approach embodied at Sodere became an established feature of subsequent Somali peace negotiations. This historical experience has direct relevance as Somalia confronts a demanding security transition, with Al-Shabaab continuing to threaten state consolidation, domestic political negotiations remaining unsettled after the inconclusive May 2026 talks, and AUSSOM’s operational future facing growing financial uncertainty following Washington’s announced intention to end its support for UN logistics and operations from 2027. Ethiopia’s renewed commitment to AUSSOM, reaffirmed at the August 2026 troop-contributing countries summit, provides an important basis for strengthening this regional security relationship. Somalia’s current security transition increases the strategic importance of sustained coordination with Ethiopia. Al-Shabaab retains a presence in areas of Gedo and Bakool near the Ethiopian frontier, while Washington’s decision to end funding for UN logistical support to AUSSOM after December 2026 adds pressure to the mission’s operational continuity. These developments connect Somalia’s internal security challenges directly to the management of its western border, where gaps in territorial control can enable armed groups to move, reorganize and exploit weaknesses in coordination between security forces. Ethiopia’s direct exposure to these threats, its existing security involvement in Somalia and its capacity to operate along the shared frontier make bilateral cooperation consequential to how these risks are managed. For Mogadishu, the practical priority is to establish predictable arrangements with Addis Ababa for intelligence exchange, border threat assessment, troop coordination and consultation over operations affecting Somali territory. These mechanisms would help align Ethiopian security activities with federal priorities, improve continuity between bilateral cooperation and AUSSOM, and give Somali authorities greater influence over the regional response to threats within their jurisdiction. As Somalia assumes greater responsibility for its own security amid uncertainty over international support, the quality of its coordination with Ethiopia will directly affect its capacity to manage cross-border threats and sustain security across its western regions. ethiopia.summary: The Sodere Initiative, launched by Ethiopia in late 1996, aimed to unify Somalia's rival factions during a period of political fragmentation following the collapse of the Somali state in 1991. Convened under the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the talks led to the establishment of a 41-member National Salvation Council, representing major clan families and smaller communities. While the initiative did not create a lasting government, it laid the groundwork for future reconciliation efforts by promoting clan-family parity in political representation. Ethiopia's involvement was driven by security concerns, particularly regarding the Islamist group Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya, which posed threats to its border. The initiative's legacy continues to influence Somalia's ongoing security challenges, particularly in light of Al-Shabaab's presence and the need for coordinated regional security efforts as Somalia transitions towards greater self-governance.

ethiopia.content: The Ethiopia-Djibouti Trade Corridor and the Shared Stakes of Regional Security – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 The Ethiopia-Djibouti Trade Corridor and the Shared Stakes of Regional Security 0 Comments The TPLF-Shabiya attempt to cut the Ethiopia-Djibouti trade corridor was more than a threat to Ethiopia’s economic lifeline; it also endangered Djibouti’s economic interests. A strategy designed to pressure the Ethiopian federal government by disrupting this vital trade route would have imposed costs on both countries, potentially extending Ethiopia’s conflict into a wider regional economic crisis. The corridor is not simply a transport link between two neighbouring states. It underpins Ethiopia’s access to international markets and Djibouti’s role as a principal gateway for Ethiopian trade. More than 95 per cent of Ethiopia’s import-export trade uses the Ethio-Djibouti corridor, while Djibouti’s economy relies heavily on Ethiopian trade through its port. A disruption would have threatened Ethiopia’s access to international markets while putting Djibouti’s port-related economic activity at risk. The scale of the impact would depend on the duration and extent of the disruption, but the corridor’s importance makes its security a shared economic concern. The plan must also be understood in the context of the military imbalance between the ENDF and the opposing forces. Given the ENDF’s apparent military superiority in conventional capabilities, direct confrontation with the Ethiopian military would have presented a significant challenge. Threatening the Ethio-Djibouti corridor could have offered the opposing forces an asymmetric means of exerting pressure on the federal government. This reflects a broader strategic logic: actors facing disadvantages in direct military confrontation may seek leverage by threatening infrastructure essential to a state’s economic functioning. The corridor represented precisely such a vulnerability. However, this strategic logic alone does not establish that a coordinated plan existed; that allegation must be assessed against the reported intelligence and subsequent battlefield developments. The corridor’s strategic significance also creates a constraint for any actor seeking to exploit it. Although disruption could impose economic costs on Ethiopia, it could simultaneously undermine Djibouti’s port revenues and commercial activity, potentially broadening opposition to the threat beyond Ethiopia’s borders. Such an outcome would risk turning an attempt to pressure the Ethiopian federal government into a wider regional security concern. The interdependence of the two economies therefore has a strategic dimension: the corridor’s vulnerability is not exclusively Ethiopia’s weakness, but also a source of shared interest in preventing its disruption. This makes the protection of the route relevant to regional stability as well as bilateral economic security. The leaked intelligence report suggests that Eritrean troops were present at 50 locations in Ethiopian territory across eastern Tigray and northern Afar before the Ethiopian government launched its defensive operation. According to the report, the deployment was intended to facilitate an attempt to cut the Ethio-Djibouti trade corridor. Subsequent reporting documented the TPLF-led forces’ advance into Afar, including the capture of Erebti and their movement towards Afdeera, underscoring the region’s strategic importance to Ethiopia’s access to Djibouti. These developments provide relevant context for assessing the alleged plan, although the reported troop deployments and rebel advances do not, on their own, establish that all the actors involved were coordinating towards that objective. The presence of Eritrean troops at these locations did not, in itself, guarantee control of the corridor. On 1 October 2026, federal forces and allied Tigray Peace Force units counterattacked and retook both towns, reversing much of the rebel advance in Afar. The ENDF’s technological capabilities, intelligence-gathering capacity and operational reach may have contributed to its response, although the extent of their influence cannot be established from the reported battlefield outcome alone. Further evidence concerning force coordination, operational decisions and battlefield performance would be needed to determine the precise factors behind the reversal. The counteroffensive addressed the immediate battlefield situation, but it did not eliminate the broader security concern raised by the alleged plan. The intelligence report therefore raises questions about foreign military deployments near strategically sensitive areas and the potential threats they could pose to Ethiopia’s economic security. The episode underscored the importance of integrating critical transport infrastructure into national defence planning, intelligence collection and inter-agency coordination. Protecting the Ethio-Djibouti corridor requires identifying vulnerabilities before armed actors can exploit them, as well as maintaining the capacity to respond effectively to emerging threats. Its geographic exposure and economic importance make early warning and infrastructure resilience essential components of corridor security. Djibouti’s position is central to this assessment. Ethiopia should therefore approach corridor protection as a shared bilateral concern rather than solely as a domestic security matter. Structured cooperation could help both countries exchange relevant threat assessments, coordinate security planning and safeguard the trade relationship on which their mutual economic interests depend. At the national level, Ethiopia should make corridor security a permanent national-security priority through complementary measures. Coordinated military and intelligence planning should strengthen strategic warning and enable authorities to assess credible indications of armed movements towards corridor-adjacent areas, suspicious troop deployments and attempts to disrupt transport networks. Layered protection should improve the resilience of critical transport and logistics infrastructure, reducing the risk that disruption at a single point could interrupt the wider trade route. Periodic reviews of security conditions and corridor vulnerabilities would help ensure that these measures remain responsive to changing threats. The security of the Ethiopia-Djibouti trade corridor is inseparable from the strategic interests of both countries. Although the ENDF’s reported counteroffensive reversed rebel gains in Afar, the alleged plan and the reported Eritrean troop deployments warrant further scrutiny. Preventing future threats requires sustained defence preparedness, effective early warning and institutionalised bilateral security cooperation. Ultimately, safeguarding the corridor is essential to Ethiopia’s economic security, Djibouti’s commercial interests and regional stability. Recent tensions, particularly the TPLF-Shabiya's attempts to disrupt this corridor, pose risks not only to Ethiopia's economic stability but also to Djibouti's port revenues. The Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) has shown military superiority, yet threats to the corridor highlight vulnerabilities that could be exploited by opposing forces. Recent military developments, including the ENDF's counteroffensive, have temporarily reversed rebel advances, but ongoing vigilance and coordinated efforts are essential to ensure the corridor's security and maintain regional stability.

ethiopia.content: Except War, What Option is Ethiopia Left With to Defend Persistent Incursions from Eritrea? – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 Except War, What Option is Ethiopia Left With to Defend Persistent Incursions from Eritrea? 0 Comments Having learned from the devastating costs of the 1998 border war between Ethiopia and Eritrea and the 2020 northern Ethiopia conflict, preventing a full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea remains crucial. In a region plagued by persistent conflict, militant activities, and extremist and terrorist havens, the last thing it needs is another war. As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated , “the last thing the world needs right now is another war.” However, Ethiopia’s relationship with Eritrea does not seem likely to be resolved through conventional diplomatic assurances alone. Since its secession, Eritrea has adopted an antagonistic posture toward its largest neighbor and pursued policies that challenge Ethiopia’s security and regional interests. It has a documented record of supporting anti-Ethiopian government armed groups, providing them with sanctuary and other forms of assistance. Following the Pretoria peace agreement, although Eritrean forces withdrew from Tigray’s heartland, they remained in territories inside Tigray near the Eritrean border. Eritrea also established an alliance with the TPLF and other armed groups inside Ethiopian territory, with the latter forming an alliance aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian federal government. In this context, Eritrea plays a significant role, while other external actors also contribute by providing support. The nature of the Eritrean state under the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ) remains a persistent source of insecurity for Ethiopia. The country’s political system is highly centralized and militarized, with indefinite national service, the dominance of military institutions over civilian administration, and the concentration of power in President Isaias Afwerki and his close circle all playing a central role in keeping the regime in power. Since the 1998–2000 border war, Eritrea has maintained a security posture shaped by permanent mobilization and a deep suspicion of Ethiopia. This reflects what can be described as a small-state syndrome, in which the perceived vulnerability of a state, its limited strategic depth, and its exposure to stronger neighbors shape how its leadership understands external threats. In Eritrea’s case, this outlook has reinforced the tendency to view Ethiopia through a security lens and to treat the preservation of regime security as a national priority. This reinforces the need to address the underlying strategic calculations that shape Eritrea’s behavior toward Ethiopia. In recent years, the practical consequences of this structure have become evident in Eritrea’s military presence in border areas of northern Ethiopia and its cultivation of relationships with armed groups operating inside Ethiopian territory. For more than a year, Ethiopian authorities documented patterns of material support, including ammunition intercepts and alleged training linkages, directed toward elements of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front and other armed groups in Ethiopia. These activities culminated in formal Ethiopian notifications to the United Nations Security Council in October 2026, invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter on the inherent right of self-defense in response to the advances of Eritrean units tens of kilometers into Tigrayan territory and coordination with domestic insurgent coalitions. The severing of diplomatic relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara in early October further removed remaining formal channels for crisis management. In this environment, Eritrea’s conduct has shifted from wartime alliance against the TPLF during 2020–2022 to a tactical realignment that treats a weakened or fragmented Ethiopian center as preferable to a consolidated neighbor capable of projecting power in the region. The nature of the regime, shaped by President Isaias Afwerki’s personalized style of rule and his longstanding political outlook towards Ethiopia, makes it unlikely that Asmara will voluntarily provide the guarantees necessary for de-escalation. For Ethiopia, however, Isaias’s decades-long rule has remained a persistent security concern, given Eritrea’s history of hostility towards its southern neighbor and its support for armed with anti-government agendas. Ethiopia needs credible guarantees from Eritrea to address these concerns, ease tensions, and create conditions for a lasting resolution. However, as noted above, the nature of Eritrea’s leadership makes such guarantees difficult to secure, particularly if they require a change in the security policies and political outlook that have shaped its approach towards Ethiopia for decades. Demands for an end to support for armed opposition groups, the cessation of cross-border arms transfers, and a verifiable halt to military preparations near Ethiopian territory would require the Eritrean leadership to reconsider practices closely tied to its system of internal control. Introduced during the 1998–2000 border war, national service has evolved into an indefinite obligation serving both military and labor needs. Many Eritreans remain in service for years, often with little control over their assignments and limited remuneration. Its prolonged nature also gives the government considerable influence over citizens’ livelihoods and their ability to leave state service. In Eritrea, generals often wield greater authority than civilian officials at the zonal level, with power ultimately concentrated in the presidency. Isaias Afwerki has also rotated military commanders and senior officials, limiting their ability to build independent power bases. Control over the economy, political coordination, information, and national security remains concentrated among a small circle of trusted figures whose influence depends heavily on their relationship with the president. Under such conditions, transparency and demobilization would be perceived as a threat to the regime’s capacity to extract resources, suppress dissent, and justify isolation. The empirical record of Eritrean foreign policy since its secession, marked by disputes with Yemen, Djibouti, Sudan, and Ethiopia, illustrates a consistent preference for confrontation over institutionalized cooperation when the latter would constrain personalist authority. In essence, full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would risk repeating the cost of the previous conflicts, while increasing the risk of regional actors becoming involved. A direct war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would be an uneven contest given Ethiopia’s demographic and military scale. Yet Eritrea’s garrison-state structure would allow it to mobilize much of its population and national resources with potentially devastating consequences for its population and economy. Therefore, Ethiopia’s dilemma would be how to neutralize the threat posed by Eritrea’s leadership without turning the military imbalance into a prolonged and costly conflict. Given these constraints, effective threat neutralization begins with identifying the specific sources of risk. These include Eritrea’s military presence, support for armed groups, and other activities directed by its leadership that threaten Ethiopia’s security. Given the concentration of political and security authority within Eritrea’s leadership, a surgical and swift operation directed at the narrow decision-making and security core offers a theoretically coherent pathway. The personalist character of the Eritrean system concentrates operational and political authority in a limited set of individuals and institutions surrounding the president. However, this approach would require a carefully defined communication strategy to establish the basis for action, build international understanding of its security concerns and demonstrate that any measures taken are necessary and proportionate to the threats identified. Israel’s approach towards Iran illustrates how operations targeting senior leadership and key decision-making structures can disrupt command arrangements and weaken a state’s capacity to coordinate its response. However, Iran’s institutional depth has allowed it to sustain resistance despite the loss of senior figures. Eritrea differs in this respect, but the case provides an illustration. Its political system is more personalized, with authority concentrated around Isaias Afwerki and a narrow circle of military and security officials. Let alone the removal of the inner circle, the removal of Isaias would be consequential extending beyond Ethiopia’s immediate security concerns, potentially reshaping Eritrea’s political order and the wider Horn of Africa. Eritrea’s relatively shallow administrative depth, compared with more layered systems that possess provincial redundancy or institutionalized revolutionary guards, may increase the disruptive potential of precise action against the center. For international actors, Eritrea’s status as a pariah state, its record of playing a spoiler role in the region, and its government’s persistent human rights violations would shape how they assess such a development. The prospect of a change in leadership could be viewed as an opportunity to address longstanding sources of regional instability and the country’s human rights crisis. In its 2015 report, the UN Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in Eritrea found that “systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations have been and are being committed in Eritrea under the authority of the Government,” adding that some of these violations “may constitute crimes against humanity.” Beyond this, such an approach could help avert a devastating interstate war, free the Eritrean people from a tyrannical and deeply oppressive regime and minimize wider humanitarian consequences. The broader regional context reinforces the logic of limitation. A major war would intersect with ongoing conflicts in Sudan, competition over Red Sea access, and Nile water disputes, creating opportunities for external actors to deeply embed themselves in the region. Eritrea’s alignment with SAF’s al-Burhan and Egypt mean that uncontrolled escalation would quickly expand the geographic and political scope of the conflict. By contrast, a tightly constrained operation that demonstrably prioritizes the neutralization of leadership-directed threats minimizes the grounds for third-party intervention and preserves Ethiopia’s capacity to address internal security challenges. The small-state syndrome that shapes Eritrean behavior is characterized by acute sensitivity to Ethiopia’s growing regional role and influence, alongside a tendency to use asymmetric means to constrain Ethiopia’s position and establish strategic buffer zones along its borders including through support for the TPLF. As noted, Eritrea’s political and security system is built around military mobilization, secrecy, and the use of regional networks to advance its strategic interests. For Ethiopia to achieve lasting security, Eritrea would need to provide credible assurances against military build-up, arms trafficking, and support for proxy groups, including the TPLF and other armed movements, while preventing its territory from being used as a sanctuary for groups seeking to destabilize Ethiopia. However, the centralized and highly personalized nature of Isaias Afwerki’s rule raises serious doubts about whether such commitments would be honored without meaningful pressure. Ethiopia’s long-term security interests therefore depend on addressing these sources of interference while avoiding the heavy costs of a prolonged interstate war. A carefully considered approach, supported by verified intelligence and a coherent communication strategy, seeks to address immediate security threats while preserving the prospects for long-term regional stability. Ethiopia cannot afford to remain trapped in the same recurring cycle of confrontation with Eritrea, in which unresolved threats repeatedly generate new tensions and bring both countries closer to a devastating war. The 1998 border war and the 2020 conflict in northern Ethiopia highlight the devastating costs of war, making conflict avoidance crucial. Eritrea's support for anti-Ethiopian armed groups and its military presence near the border exacerbate tensions. Opening the three-day capacity development workshop today, Ethiopia's Auditor General Meseret Damtie said strengthening African Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) is essential in order to promote accountable governance, sound public financial management and sustainable development across the continent. She emphasized that improved audit quality, institutional capacity and collaboration are essential to enable audit institutions fulfil their mandates effectively. "At the heart of ARISE (African Regional Initiative for Strengthening Effectiveness) is the spirit of peer support and collaboration," the Auditor General said, highlighting the importance of cooperation among participating institutions, programme coordinators, peer SAIs and development partners in achieving sustainable results. Meseret linked the principles of cooperation and collective responsibility underpinning ARISE to Ethiopia's Medemer philosophy, which emphasizes synergy, shared contributions and common goals. She highlighted the importance of collaboration in strengthening institutions and advancing sustainable development, reflecting the program's emphasis on partnerships and collective efforts to improve public-sector accountability across Africa. INTOSAI Development Initiative (IDI) representative, Muhammed Dabo, stressed that sustainable improvements in Supreme Audit Institutions require more than technical training, emphasizing strong institutional systems, effective leadership, capable personnel and the ability to manage change. "Each partner has a distinct role, but we share one objective: stronger, more effective and sustainable Supreme Audit Institutions," he said, underscoring the complementary roles of beneficiary SAIs, peer institutions, regional organizations and development partners. Dabo encouraged the participants to share experiences openly, identify challenges early, adapt when necessary and develop practical solutions for their respective institutions. He stressed that the workshop's success should be measured by the lessons applied and improvements achieved after participants return to their work. INTOSAI Development Initiative representative, Muhammed Dabo, highlighted that sustainable improvements require strong institutional systems and effective leadership. During an interview with the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), he said the TPLF violated the Pretoria Agreement signed in October 2022. The PM recalled that the key elements of the Pretoria Agreement included cessation of hostilities, restoration of all services, disarmament, return of displaced people, and recognition of the constitutional order. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The federal government had fulfilled everything that was possible and expected of it, he added. On the contrary, the TPLF had been purchasing and soliciting weapons as well as openly recruiting young people instead of implementing the agreement to disarm combatants. Above all, PM Abiy pointed out that after the agreement, the TPLF used displaced persons as hostages to prevent them from returning to their homes. Additionally, it engaged in destroying and closing down infrastructure--including airlines, banking, and telecommunications--that had been restored by the Federal Government to deliver services. Despite the group's misdeeds, the PM stated that the government had forewarned that war was not worthwhile and that peace was preferable. However, the TPLF disregarded the advice and collaborated with various forces, and violated the Pretoria Agreement by initiating an unnecessary war. Immense damage has been inflicted on the public as a result of the war instigated by the TPLF, he noted. War is bad and yields no benefit, the Premier further noted, adding that a war fought for the interests of foreign forces is even worse. The psychological damage is not to be taken lightly and damage has also been inflicted on development and the economy. PM Abiy stressed that young people carrying Kalashnikovs should therefore return to work and participate in the development and rehabilitation of Tigray. Noting that many young people were forcibly recruited, he advised those who have not yet returned to return to normal life. He stated that the leaders of the TPLF have been declaring war for 50 years without dying or being wounded themselves; instead they sent their children and families abroad and to Addis Ababa where they are engaged in business and construction. The Premier highlighted the shared legacy of courage, unity, and sacrifice between the two countries. In a social media post, the Prime Minister said: "I delivered remarks paying tribute to the heroes who fought for freedom and those who made the ultimate sacrifices to safeguard their nation. I honour their courage and legacy!" PM Abiy noted that Kenya's history of courage and sacrifice resonates deeply with Ethiopia's own story of Adwa, where Ethiopians from every corner of the country united to defend their homeland. These shared histories remind us that freedom was never given but won through courage, unity, and sacrifice, the Prime Minister added. "As our histories are intertwined, so too must our futures be. Through the spirit of Medemer, Ethiopia and Kenya must continue building on our existing cooperation in clean energy, connectivity, telecommunications, and trade to create greater opportunities and shared prosperity for our people," he said. The two countries also cooperate in regional security, cross-border infrastructure, trade, telecommunications, and electricity interconnections, supporting economic integration and development across the Horn of Africa, it was learned. Taye underscored the importance of reliable statistics in driving evidence-based development in Africa. Addressing the opening of the 10th Session of the Statistical Commission for Africa and the 12th Meeting of the Regional Committee of the United Nations Global Geospatial Information Management for Africa in Addis Ababa, the President said Ethiopia's development planning is anchored in measurable targets and reliable data. He emphasized that development cannot be effectively planned, sustained, or scaled up without accurate measurement, noting that official statistics are essential for shaping development strategies, tracking progress, and strengthening accountability. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The President also highlighted Ethiopia's reforms in the financial and digital sectors, including the National Digital Payment Strategy, financial sector liberalization, interoperable payment infrastructure, and the national digital identification program, Fayda. He said Fayda enables secure electronic verification and expands access to banking, mobile money, telecommunications, and other essential public services, demonstrating how digital infrastructure can improve service delivery and financial inclusion. According to the President, mobile money and mobile banking accounts in Ethiopia reached 257 million and processed more than 24 trillion birr in transactions during the first nine months of 2026, reflecting the expansion of the country's financial and digital systems. Drawing lessons from these reforms, he stressed that statistics must serve as practical tools for sustainable development and be communicated clearly and accessibly to policymakers and citizens, rather than being treated as an end in themselves. He also called for statistical institutions to integrate and safeguard diverse data sources without compromising statistical integrity, emphasizing that innovation must reinforce data quality, institutional independence, and public trust. The President urged African governments to protect the professional independence of official statistics, strengthen legal and institutional frameworks, invest in national statistical systems, and ground policy decisions in scientific evidence. He cautioned that poor-quality data undermines evidence-based policymaking, impedes development, and weakens accountability. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: News - Funding Shortfalls Threaten Health Services in Ethiopia's Conflict-Hit Regions, UN Warns - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: News - Funding Shortfalls Threaten Health Services in Ethiopia's Conflict-Hit Regions, UN Warns 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Funding shortages threaten essential health and nutrition services in Ethiopia's conflict-affected regions, with 10 of the 16 operational mobile health and nutrition teams in Amhara expected to shut down by the end of October, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said. According to OCHA , only 16 of the 57 mobile health and nutrition teams required in Amhara are currently operational. Of these, 10 are expected to cease operations by the end of the month because of funding constraints. Humanitarian partners are continuing to deliver life-saving assistance despite insecurity and access challenges in parts of northern Ethiopia, including Tigray, Amhara and Afar, the UN agency said. In Tigray, additional medical, nutrition and other essential supplies have reached communities and health facilities, with further deliveries expected. Humanitarian partners are also working with regional authorities to facilitate access and expand assistance. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn On Tuesday, Humanitarian Coordinator in Ethiopia Ozonnia Ojielo met officials from the newly established caretaker interim administration in Tigray, emphasizing the need for unhindered humanitarian access, according to OCHA. In Amhara, humanitarian partners are preparing to provide food assistance to approximately 100,000 people in Wag Hamra and North Wollo zones. Operations are also continuing in Afar, although limited funding remains a major obstacle to expanding the response. OCHA said humanitarian needs across Ethiopia continue to exceed available resources, warning that funding shortfalls are undermining efforts to sustain essential services for vulnerable communities. The agency reiterated its call for all parties to facilitate the expansion of life-saving humanitarian assistance and ensure humanitarian actors can reach people in need. The funding shortfall extends beyond health services, affecting food assistance, refugee protection and support for internally displaced people (IDPs), as previously reported by Addis Standard. Earlier this month, Addis Standard reported that IDPs in camps in Debre Birhan were facing worsening shortages of food, medicines, healthcare and other essential services as humanitarian organizations scaled back or withdrew operations amid funding constraints. Continued displacement from conflict-affected areas has further strained already limited resources. The situation reflects a broader displacement crisis across Amhara. As of early 2025, more than 660,000 people were estimated to be living in 31 IDP sites and collective centres across seven administrative zones, with North and South Wollo accounting for approximately 55% of the sites. Major displacement locations include the Bakelo and China camps in Debre Birhan and the Jara IDP Centre in North Wollo. ethiopia.title: Eritrea Tells Us There Is No 'Crisis' Between Ethiopia and Eritrea
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Eritrea Tells Us There Is No 'Crisis' Between Ethiopia and Eritrea - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Eritrea Tells Us There Is No 'Crisis' Between Ethiopia and Eritrea 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Eritrea's Ambassador to the United Nations, Sophia Tesfamariam, has told senior US diplomats that there is no "crisis" between Ethiopia and Eritrea, while urging Washington and other international actors to address what she described as threats to Eritrea's sovereignty and territorial integrity. In a statement posted on X on 20 October, Sophia said she held "constructive engagements" with Mike Waltz, the US permanent representative to the UN, and Jeffrey Bartos, the US representative to the UN for Management and Reform, to discuss developments in the Horn of Africa and present Asmara's position on the region's deteriorating security situation. Over the last two weeks, the two countries exchanged accusations at the United Nations over their deteriorating relations. Ethiopia sent a letter to the UN Security Council in early October accusing Eritrean forces of an "all-out invasion" of parts of Tigray in northern Ethiopia and invoking its right to self-defence. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Eritrea rejected Ethiopia's account and, in its own communication to the Council, accused Addis Abeba of threatening a war of aggression over Red Sea access. The two governments' competing accounts have emerged alongside renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia and heightened fears of a broader regional conflict. Sophia said she had "reiterated that there is no 'crisis' between Eritrea and Ethiopia" and argued that the international community should pay closer attention to developments within Ethiopia. She urged Addis Abeba to "respect Eritrea's sovereign territories and stop diverting attention from its domestic issues." The ambassador also accused Ethiopia of pursuing a three-year campaign concerning access to the Red Sea and making continued threats against Eritrea's sovereignty, including what she described as threats to annex Eritrean territory. She called on countries with influence in the region to act "responsibly and proactively" to prevent a wider conflict, cautioning them against making statements that could embolden Ethiopia's leadership. "Eritrea's sovereignty and territorial integrity must be respected," she said, adding that preventing renewed conflict requires addressing underlying threats, upholding international law and acting before tensions escalate. Convened in late 1996 under IGAD’s newly established conflict-resolution mandate, the talks culminated on 3 January 1997 in the creation of a 41-member National Salvation Council, with representation allocated to the four major clan families and smaller communities. Although Sodere did not produce a lasting government, it established a broad-based framework for political representation that subsequent reconciliation efforts would revisit The collapse of the Somali state in January 1991 left political authority dispersed among armed factions, while successive international efforts failed to establish a national government capable of consolidating control. The Addis Ababa Agreement of 1993 brought leading factions into a common framework, but agreement on paper did not resolve the struggle for power in Mogadishu; by the time the last United Nations troops withdrew in March 1995, the underlying competition remained intact. Rivalry between Ali Mahdi Mohamed and the Aideed camp, which passed to Hussein Aideed following General Mohamed Farah Aideed’s death in August 1996, continued to obstruct the emergence of a national political authority. The consequences extended beyond the capital. In the border region of Gedo, Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI) established a presence centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometers from Ethiopia, which Addis Ababa regarded as a base for a movement responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linked to other armed groups opposed to its government. Somalia’s fragmentation thus presented Ethiopia with a problem that international mediation alone had not resolved, the absence of a functioning state was not merely prolonging conflict within Somalia but also leaving neighboring territory exposed to armed networks that could operate across the border. This gave Ethiopia a direct security interest in the restoration of Somali political authority. The expansion of regional institutions in 1996 provided an important foundation for a more coordinated response to Somalia’s political fragmentation, creating a framework through which Ethiopia could address its security concerns while contributing to a regional effort to restore Somali political dialogue. Founded in 1986 as the Intergovernmental Authority on Drought and Development, with a mandate centred on drought and desertification, the organization was reconstituted as the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) following the amendment of its founding instrument in Nairobi on 21 March 1996 and its relaunch at the Djibouti summit of 25–26 November. The revised charter incorporated the prevention, management and resolution of inter-state and intra-state conflicts through dialogue, placing peace and security alongside food security and economic cooperation among the organization’s priorities. This change reflected a broader recognition that the conflicts confronting the Horn of Africa required regional mechanisms capable of addressing their political and security dimensions. For Ethiopia, whose border security was directly affected by the absence of effective authority in Somalia, IGAD’s expanded mandate offered a legitimate avenue for supporting reconciliation through regional diplomacy. The framework connected Ethiopia’s immediate security concerns with the wider regional interest in reducing conflict and restoring political order in Somalia, giving its diplomatic engagement an institutional foundation and a shared regional purpose. Although divisions among IGAD members, including the severance of relations with Sudan by Ethiopia, Eritrea and Uganda during the preceding year, complicated regional cooperation, the organization’s expanded mandate established an important basis for renewed engagement. OAU strengthened this framework in July 1996, when its Yaoundé resolution recognized Meles Zenawi, then outgoing OAU chairman, as holding a special mandate to facilitate peace in Somalia and supported efforts by IGAD member states to reactivate their initiatives. This endorsement connected the emerging regional effort to the OAU’s broader diplomatic role and reinforced the legitimacy of renewed attempts to bring Somali factions into negotiations. Ethiopia subsequently informed the United Nations Security Council that it had convened the Sodere conference in November 1996 in accordance with an IGAD mandate. Operating within this reinforced regional framework, Ethiopian conduct in the second half of 1996 ran along two tracks that differed in instrument yet converged through local partnerships. On the military track, Ethiopia acted against Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI), an Islamist group that had established a presence in the Gedo region centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometres from the Ethiopian border. Addis Ababa regarded AIAI as a direct security threat, holding it responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linking it to other armed networks opposed to the Ethiopian government. Ethiopian forces therefore crossed into Gedo on 9 August 1996 to attack AIAI bases, and fighting continued through December. The fourth major assault on the group, launched on 11 June 1997, captured Luuq and Buulo Haawo and deprived AIAI of its last major bases in the region. This military campaign ran in parallel with a political initiative that sought to harness Somali opposition to AIAI and embed Ethiopia’s border-security objectives within a broader reconciliation process. On the political track, Ethiopia convened Somali leaders at the Sodere resort for roughly six weeks of talks, which ended on 3 January 1997 with a declaration signed by 27 leaders representing 26 factions. The declaration created a National Salvation Council of 41 members and a National Executive Committee of 11 members led by five co-chairmen, with authority to speak for the Council and to prepare a Transitional Central Authority or Provisional Central Government, and it committed the signatories to a National Reconciliation Conference at Bossaso. The Somali National Front, a competitor of AIAI for control of Gedo, was among the signatories. That overlap offered Somali opponents of AIAI an institutional route to national standing and tied a border security objective to a political process that Somali actors could own. The composition of the Council contains the process’s most durable contribution. Nine seats went to each of the four major clan families, Darod, Hawiye, Rahanweyn and Dir, and five to smaller groups, a distribution that totals 41 and approximates the half-share later formalized for minorities under the 4.5 formula. For the first time the Darod accepted parity among the main clan families. That principle of clan-family parity, first given institutional expression at Sodere, was subsequently formalized at the Arta conference in 2000 and then applied at scale by the Mbagathi process, which in 2004 allocated 61 seats to each of the four major families and 31 to the minority bloc within a 275-member Transitional Federal Parliament. By converting a contest over who speaks for Somalia into a bounded negotiation over who sits within each family’s allotment, parity supplied the mechanism through which Sodere moved Somali politics from open military competition toward transitional institutions. Sodere’s significance extended beyond the representational framework it helped establish to the regional diplomacy through which that framework was pursued. Ethiopia’s subsequent involvement in Somali reconciliation formed part of a recurring pattern that included hosting the 1993 Addis Ababa conference, convening Sodere in 1996 and 1997, participating in the IGAD-mediated Mbagathi talks that produced the Transitional Federal Charter in 2004, and contributing troops to the African Union missions in Somalia, AMISOM and ATMIS, and now AUSSOM. The Mbagathi record offers particularly clear evidence that Somali actors themselves regarded Ethiopia’s participation as consequential. In February 2004, six faction leaders of the Somali Restoration and Reconstruction Council announced that they would stay out of the final phase of the talks while Ethiopia was absent from the table. Hussein Aideed, who had succeeded his father General Mohamed Farah Aideed in 1996 and had remained outside the Sodere process the following year, now argued that a regional peace process required consensus among neighbouring states as well as among Somalis. His position marked a shift from contesting Ethiopia’s involvement in 1997 to treating the participation of neighboring states as a condition of a credible settlement, illustrating how the regional approach embodied at Sodere became an established feature of subsequent Somali peace negotiations. This historical experience has direct relevance as Somalia confronts a demanding security transition, with Al-Shabaab continuing to threaten state consolidation, domestic political negotiations remaining unsettled after the inconclusive May 2026 talks, and AUSSOM’s operational future facing growing financial uncertainty following Washington’s announced intention to end its support for UN logistics and operations from 2027. Ethiopia’s renewed commitment to AUSSOM, reaffirmed at the August 2026 troop-contributing countries summit, provides an important basis for strengthening this regional security relationship. Somalia’s current security transition increases the strategic importance of sustained coordination with Ethiopia. Al-Shabaab retains a presence in areas of Gedo and Bakool near the Ethiopian frontier, while Washington’s decision to end funding for UN logistical support to AUSSOM after December 2026 adds pressure to the mission’s operational continuity. These developments connect Somalia’s internal security challenges directly to the management of its western border, where gaps in territorial control can enable armed groups to move, reorganize and exploit weaknesses in coordination between security forces. Ethiopia’s direct exposure to these threats, its existing security involvement in Somalia and its capacity to operate along the shared frontier make bilateral cooperation consequential to how these risks are managed. For Mogadishu, the practical priority is to establish predictable arrangements with Addis Ababa for intelligence exchange, border threat assessment, troop coordination and consultation over operations affecting Somali territory. These mechanisms would help align Ethiopian security activities with federal priorities, improve continuity between bilateral cooperation and AUSSOM, and give Somali authorities greater influence over the regional response to threats within their jurisdiction. As Somalia assumes greater responsibility for its own security amid uncertainty over international support, the quality of its coordination with Ethiopia will directly affect its capacity to manage cross-border threats and sustain security across its western regions. Convened under the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the talks led to the establishment of a 41-member National Salvation Council, representing major clan families and smaller communities. While the initiative did not create a lasting government, it laid the groundwork for future reconciliation efforts by promoting clan-family parity in political representation. The initiative's legacy continues to influence Somalia's ongoing security challenges, particularly in light of Al-Shabaab's presence and the need for coordinated regional security efforts as Somalia transitions towards greater self-governance.
