All rights reserved. An interview with Ali Omar, by Callum McFadden for WFi . You are a regular international with Somalia. How proud are you to represent your country, and how does playing on the international stage compare with club football? Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "Representing my national team is honestly the best feeling in the world. There are certain things you cannot describe unless you have experienced them yourself. "To be given the opportunity to play against some of the best superstars in the world is incredible. I was saying to the lads the other day that the transition from playing for Dumbarton to representing Somalia is crazy. I go from playing in front of 800 people every week to playing in front of between 40,000 and 70,000 people at international level. "You have to come out of one bubble and go into another. You are living in two different realities. One minute you are flying high, and the next you are back at your club, where things are completely different. You have to learn to adapt and switch between those environments quickly. "For me, being able to represent my country and give everything for my nation is the best feeling in the world. There is nothing quite like it." Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement What have been the highlights of your international career so far, and who are the best players you have faced? "I have two main highlights. The first was playing against Algeria. Two hours before the game, there were 70,000 people in the stadium. I could not believe it. The passion from the fans and the build-up were extraordinary. "That night I was playing against Riyad Mahrez. Honestly, it was unbelievable. Every time he touched the ball, you would think God had come down. That is how loud it was. The noise was incredible, and you could immediately see why he has had a world-class career. His touch was immaculate, and he was calm under any pressure. "Another big moment was playing against Ivory Coast a couple of weeks ago. I had to pinch myself as I was facing some of the best players in the world, including players such as Yan Diomande, who has just joined Real Madrid for over £100 million, and other quality players such as Nicolas Pépé and Franck Kessié. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "For someone like me, coming from little Dumbarton and then playing against some of the biggest names in world football, it is a massive experience. I feel incredibly lucky and grateful for the opportunities I have been given. "I always tell people that, if you get the chance to represent your country, whatever country that may be, take it and give everything you have. These opportunities do not come around often." You have made a significant impact since joining Dumbarton, both as a defender and as a leader. The club was going through a difficult period when you arrived, but results have improved. How do you reflect on that progress? "When I first came to the club, we were going through a rough patch. But, as we both know, things can always turn around. I felt it was only a matter of time. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "I remember playing against Clyde on a Tuesday night and drawing 0-0. When we got back into the dressing room, I called my family and spoke to the owner. I told them that I guaranteed we were going to go on an amazing run because I could feel something within the group. "We then went on a nine-game unbeaten run. The players had given us something to build on, and we secured our place in the league after the club had gone through administration. "We have also made a good start to this season. We have 12 points and are sitting three points off the play-offs, so you can see the progress we are making. We are not where we want to be yet, but these things take time because we are still a relatively new squad. "Unfortunately, we are currently in the process of changing manager following some difficult circumstances this season, so hopefully we can continue building on what we have started and get Dumbarton where we want to be. That is the goal." Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement You have also become a popular figure among the Dumbarton supporters. What does the relationship you have built with the fans and the local community mean to you? "Honestly, the love and appreciation I have for the fans is massive. From the moment I arrived, the club and the people around Dumbarton have made me feel so welcome, and that is something I will never take for granted. "One of the things that means the most to me is seeing the kids who come to watch us. From the warm-up right through to the match itself, they are always cheering my name. For me, that is an incredible feeling. You do not take those moments for granted because you understand what it means to those young supporters to have someone they can look up to. "I always try to make time for the fans after games, and when I see people around the local area, I make sure I speak to them as well. It is important to me because football is about more than what happens on the pitch. The supporters give you so much encouragement, and I want them to know that I appreciate every bit of it. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "Dumbarton and the community have become really important to me because of how welcoming everyone has been. When you feel that kind of love and support, you want to give something back. Whether that is through my performances, taking time to speak to the kids, or simply having a conversation with someone in the town, I want people to know how much I value them. "The fans are a massive part of what makes this club special. They are there supporting us, and I want to do everything I can to make them proud." How have you found playing in Scottish football so far? "My first thought when I arrived was that I did not think I was going to last because of the weather! Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "Seriously, on a Saturday afternoon, it can be so windy that you try to play a diagonal pass and the ball rolls back towards you. You wonder what is going on. "But the beautiful thing is that you adapt to your environment and become accustomed to it. "What I find fascinating about Scottish football is how few teams there are in each league and how often you play one another. You can face the same team four times in a season, which was something I had never experienced before. "The margins are also so small. You can be two or three wins away from the top of the table, the bottom of the table, or a play-off place. It is crazy how quickly things can change. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "You keep seeing the same faces, and you want to do everything you can to get the results. It is a completely different experience from what I was used to, and that is what makes it so fascinating." You came through the youth system at Stevenage before spending time at Queens Park Rangers. What did you learn from those experiences? "The biggest thing I learned at Stevenage was that you have to be mentally strong. You need resilience because things can change so quickly in football. "From my time as a scholar at Stevenage through to my first year at QPR, I learned the importance of patience and controlling your emotions. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "When you are young, you do not always understand why certain things happen or why things do not go your way. You might play one week and not the next. You gradually learn how to deal with those situations as you mature. "Now, at the age I am, I understand why I had to go through certain experiences at Stevenage and QPR. They helped shape me into the person I am today. "I am still not the person I want to become, but those experiences are helping me develop. Hopefully, over the next two, three, four, or five years, I will continue to grow. "Football comes with ups and downs. What I have learned is to enjoy the good times and learn from the difficult ones, because the downs do not last forever. Everything I have experienced has helped mould me into the person I am today." Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement You made a big move to Irish League Champions Larne after playing around 65 games for Torquay United, but injuries interrupted your progress in Northern Ireland. How frustrating was that setback? "I played almost 65 games for Torquay in the National League, which earned me the move to Larne, who were in European football at the time. "Unfortunately, while at Larne, I suffered an MCL injury which set me back, and I was not able to make the impact at the club that I would have liked." Although you would never have wanted to get injured, you have previously said that the experience changed you as a person and an athlete. What did you learn from it? Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "When I speak to people about my injury, I tell them that, although I am not happy it happened, in some ways I am glad it did because it created a different person. "When I got injured, I learned a lot about myself and my body. I learned what I could and could not do, and I learned about rehabilitation, nutrition, and sleep. All those things are essential parts of the recovery process. "I do not want to sound negative, but I feel the injury happened for a reason. If it had never happened, perhaps I would not have the mindset I have today. "It made me realise how important it is to look after my body, fuel it properly, and go to the gym four or five times a week. The injury helped me become the athlete I am today because I understand that I need to be strong in every area to maintain my fitness. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "I wanted to learn more about the gym and understand my body better. Thankfully, I have not had any injuries since then, and I am feeling healthy and fit." Finally, Ali, you are 27 and arguably approaching your peak years. How excited are you about the next stage of your career, both at club level and with Somalia? "I have told my friends and family that I feel I could play until I am 40. I look after my body, pay close attention to what I eat and make sure I get to the gym regularly. "My injury taught me that these things are essential for a footballer. I know I am doing well, but I also know I can do better. I have set myself short-, medium-, and long-term targets. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "With Somalia, the goal is to qualify for the Africa Cup of Nations. If we do not manage it this time, I genuinely believe we can achieve it in the future. "You can see the development within the national team. We are bringing in better players, and people who have not previously been called up are showing an interest because of the results we have been achieving. "We have World Cup qualifiers coming up, and one of the things I love about football is that you never know what can happen. Anyone can beat anyone on their day. "Nobody would have predicted that little Somalia would take Ivory Coast to the 90th minute at 0-0. That shows what is possible. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "Hopefully, in the near future, we can qualify for the Africa Cup of Nations and potentially the World Cup. "At club level, my ambition is to reach the highest level possible. Whether that is within the SPFL, English football, or another league in Europe, I want to give myself the best possible chance of getting there. "I want to know that I have given everything I possibly can to achieve my goals. If I never reach that level, I want to be able to look back and say I did my very best. If I do get there, I will know I deserve it because I have put in the hard work. "For me, that is the most important thing."
somalia.summary: Ali Omar, a defender for Dumbarton and a regular international player for Somalia, expressed immense pride in representing his country, highlighting the stark contrast between club and international football. He described the thrill of playing in front of large crowds and facing world-class players like Riyad Mahrez and those from Ivory Coast. Omar reflected on his journey, noting the challenges and growth he experienced at clubs like Stevenage and QPR, as well as the setbacks from injuries during his time at Larne. He emphasized the importance of resilience and adaptability in football, particularly in the unique environment of Scottish football. Omar also cherishes his connection with Dumbarton fans, appreciating their support and aiming to give back to the community. Looking ahead, he is excited about his career's next phase and aims to help Somalia qualify for major tournaments.

In a statement, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said projections developed with the Danish Refugee Council estimate that 874,319 people could be displaced between October and December, with flooding accounting for 92% of the total. “We are looking at the possibility of hundreds of thousands of people losing their homes in just a matter of weeks,” said Manuel Marques Pereira, IOM Somalia chief of mission. The warning comes as Somalia enters a rainy season forecast to bring above-normal rainfall amid strengthening El Nino conditions. IOM said it has secured only 14.4% of the $16.62 million required to prepare for and respond to flooding, with the funding intended to assist more than 517,000 people. Beletweyne and Gaalkacyo face particularly “greatest threat,” with nearly 229,000 and 82,000 people, respectively, at risk of displacement. The agency said rising river levels and heavy rainfall are already threatening communities, while flooding could destroy crops, contaminate water sources and disrupt access to healthcare. somalia.content: Somalia’s Misattribution of Security Failure and the fonts of Federal Overreach – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 Somalia’s Misattribution of Security Failure and the fonts of Federal Overreach 0 Comments The federal government of Somalia under Hassan Sheikh Mohamud faces a legitimacy crisis of its own making in the South West State and its response has followed a predictable pattern with the militarization of an internal political dispute, the securitization of a regional rival and the externalization of blame on to neighbouring states. The sequence of events beginning in March 2026 and culminating in the territorial collapse around Baidoa in October reveals a structural failure within Somalia’s federal system rather than an externally orchestrated conspiracy. The rhetorical turn against Kenya and Ethiopia functions less as an accurate diagnosis of the crisis than as a mechanism of political damage control and the evidence suggests that the core dysfunction is internal to Somalia’s constitutional order rather than located in the behaviour of its neighbours. The origins of the current confrontation are domestic and constitutional. In late March 2026 federal forces entered Baidoa and forcibly removed South West State President Abdiaziz Laftagareen following a dispute over election timing and constitutional revisions. Laftagareen had defied Mogadishu’s electoral plans and organized a snap re election prompting the federal government to deploy military reinforcements from Buur Hakaba into the regional capital. The intervention succeeded tactically with Laftagareen resigned and departed for Nairobi and by June a loyalist Aden Madobe had been installed through a regional parliamentary vote. What Mogadishu did not secure however was the political legitimacy of the replacement administration or the acquiescence of Laftagareen’s constituency. This distinction between tactical success and political consolidation is central to understanding everything that followed because it exposes a structural gap in the federal government’s theory of change that the assumption that control of the capital and the installation of a pliant administration constitute effective governance. That assumption is empirically false in federal systems where regional authority rests on locally embedded legitimacy rather than central appointment. The consequences of that legitimacy deficit became visible in mid October . Forces loyal to the ousted leader rapidly seized several key towns in the Bay region including Buurhakaba, Qansaxdheere, Berdale, Dinsoor and Awdinle. Most of these advances encountered minimal resistance with local officials reportedly fled to African Union bases and Ethiopian troops stationed nearby did not intervene. Baidoa itself is now effectively isolated. The speed of the collapse indicates not that Laftagareen commands a formidable military machine but that the federally installed administration in Baidoa lacks rooted local support. When a regional government can be displaced from most of its territory within days by a force that was until recently in exile, the problem is one of political legitimacy rather than external aggression. The territorial reversals are a symptom of a governance deficit, not a military one and the causal mechanism runs from legitimacy to territorial control rather than in the reverse direction. Mogadishu’s response to this reversal has been to reframe a political setback as a counterterrorism emergency. The National Committee for Combating Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism added Laftagareen, former Custodial Corps commander Mahad Shub and eight others to a financial sanctions list over suspected links to Al Shabaab . The committee stated that the designations were based on assessed evidence of financial support for the militant group but the published decision did not disclose the specific evidence against each individual. This evidentiary opacity is not incidental and it is structurally necessary to the deflection strategy. A sanctions regime that operates without public evidentiary standards allows the government to impose material costs on political rivals while maintaining the rhetorical cover of counterterrorism. The designation functions as a political instrument dressed in security terminology and its effectiveness depends precisely on the absence of the evidentiary transparency that would ordinarily accompany criminal or terrorist designation. The externalization of blame followed immediately. Parliamentary Speaker Abdikadir Jama criticized Ethiopia for allegedly standing by as forces seized towns where Ethiopian troops were deployed and accused Kenya of hosting sanctioned individuals. The speaker demanded that the federal government seek explanations from Ethiopian troops serving under AUSSOM and questioned how Al Shabaab could capture areas where Ethiopian forces were present. These accusations perform a specific political function: they shift the locus of accountability from Mogadishu’s failed intervention to the supposed negligence or complicity of its neighbours. In structural terms, this is a classic externalization move in which domestic institutional failure is recoded as foreign sabotage. The move is analytically distinguishable from a genuine security assessment because it proceeds without a corresponding investigation, without evidentiary disclosure and without any adjustment to the federal governments own operational posture in the affected areas. The reality of the neighbouring states positions is considerably more mundane and does not support the conspiracy narrative. Kenya has historically served as a political space for Somali actors across the spectrum and no bilateral extradition treaty exists between Nairobi and Mogadishu. Kenyan authorities have resisted pressure to hand over Laftagareen but this reflects a policy of hosting Somali political figures rather than a deliberate campaign to destabilize Somalia. kenya’s posture is consistent with its regional role as a venue for Somali political accommodation not with active sponsorship of insurgency. Ethiopian commanders in the Bay and Bakool regions have reportedly declined to join the political war against Laftagareen citing their counterterrorism mandate under AUSSOM. The Ethiopian position is that its troops are deployed to fight Al Shabaab not to adjudicate Somali elite power struggles. This is a defensible reading of a peace enforcement mandate not evidence of hostile intent. Neither neighbour is actively running the insurgency and both are declining to fully subordinate their mandates to political objectives. The distinction between non subordination and hostility is crucial because the federal government’s rhetoric systematically collapses the two. The structural dimensions of the crisis extend beyond South West State. Puntland and Jubaland have both expressed opposition to Mogadishu’s constitutional and electoral reforms and the pattern of central overreach followed by regional resistance is replicating across federal member states. The South West intervention was not an isolated act of strong governance and it was the first major expression of a broader centralizing impulse that treats federalism as an obstacle to be managed rather than a constitutional framework to be negotiated. When the federal government chose military force over political negotiation it signaled that the constitutional division of powers was subordinate to presidential preference. This precedent has implications beyond Bay and Bakool because it establishes a template for center region relations that other federal member states can reasonably expect to face. The replication pattern suggests that the South West episode is not an aberration but a structural feature of the current federal government’s approach to center region relations. The labeling of political rivals as terrorists is a familiar structural move in states where institutional mechanisms for resolving intra government disputes are weak or absent. When the constitutional order provides no effective forum for negotiating power sharing between the center and regions and when electoral processes are manipulated or rejected by the center, the incentives for securitizing political opposition become overwhelming. The federal government’s sanctions list and its parliamentary speaker’s accusations against Kenya and Ethiopia should be read in this light. They are not analytical descriptions of the conflict but they are instruments in it. The securitization of domestic opponents serves three functions simultaneously, it delegitimizes rivals, it justifies coercive measures that would otherwise require judicial process and it creates an external scapegoat for outcomes that are internally generated. Each of these functions is separable from the others and each can be evaluated on its own terms but their combination produces a self reinforcing cycle in which political failure generates securitization, securitization generates external blame and external blame generates further political failure by foreclosing negotiation. The core problem is not Kenyan or Ethiopian machination. It is a federal system in which the center has demonstrated a willingness to use military force against regional leaders has installed replacement administrations with shallow local roots and has then attributed the predictable consequences of those choices to foreign interference. The anti Kenya and anti Ethiopia rhetoric is damage control, an attempt to reframe a self inflicted political crisis as a story of external betrayal. Kenya and Ethiopia are not actively running the insurgency and they are simply refusing to fully subordinate themselves to Mogadishu’s political goals and that refusal is being recoded as hostility. Until Mogadishu confronts the structural deficiencies in its approach to federalism , the absence of genuine negotiation, the reliance on coercion and the legitimacy gap of its installed allies, the pattern will repeat. The towns around Baidoa are not the last to be lost to this logic and the neighbours will continue to serve as convenient explanations for failures that originate closer to home. More than 100 delegates from Uganda are attending alongside 146 Somali representatives. The gathering includes a review of previous agreements, a business forum and a joint exhibition. The meeting follows the inaugural session of the Somalia–Uganda Joint Permanent Commission, held in Kampala on 7–8 October 2025. Delegations are now assessing progress on earlier commitments and identifying challenges affecting their implementation. Ongoing discussions cover security, defence, labour, health, energy, fisheries, finance, transport, civil aviation, tourism, product standards and statistics. A bilateral labour agreement is among the proposed documents scheduled for signing, alongside other agreements concerning air services, military training, customs, health and statistics. It has not yet been confirmed which agreements have been formally signed. Related articles Somalia, Uganda Agree on Free Visas on Arrival for Diplomatic and Service Passport Holders El Niño: WMO, OCHA Call for Urgent Action to Protect People Most at Risk The business forum is also showcasing investment and trade opportunities, with presentations scheduled from Uganda Airlines, SOMINVEST and investment promotion institutions. Uganda has long supported Somalia in the security sector, while both countries are also members of the East African Community (EAC), which Somalia joined in 2024. According to the official programme, discussions will continue on 22 October, when delegates are scheduled to endorse agreed outcomes and sign the Mogadishu Declaration on bilateral investment and trade cooperation. The agreement was signed on Tuesday in Wuhu, the city in China's Anhui province where Chery is based, between Chery Overseas Investment Corp. and Dahabshiil Motors, the group's vehicle unit. It makes Dahabshiil Motors an authorized Chery dealer in Somalia and includes warranty coverage for buyers, the Somali Embassy in China said in a statement announcing the deal. Hodan Osman Abdi, Somalia's ambassador to China, attended the signing and congratulated both companies. The embassy said the partnership would give Somali consumers access to Chery vehicles backed by warranty services and would strengthen commercial ties between Somali businesses and Chinese manufacturers. The terms of the deal and the Chery models that will be offered were not disclosed. A growing car business Dahabshiil Motors was set up in 2019, when it brought Hyundai to Somaliland as the South Korean carmaker's sole distributor in the Somali regions. It opened with eight Hyundai models, including the Santa Fe, Tucson, Creta and Elantra, along with a commercial bus and a light truck, and built repair and service workshops to support them. Buyers could pay in cash or take Islamic murabaha financing from the group's bank. The unit, which operates in Somaliland and Somalia, has since added Toyota, BYD, JMC and Sinotruk to its range and now sells new vehicles, spare parts, servicing and financing. Chery is its fourth Chinese brand, after BYD, JMC and Sinotruk. Chery, founded in 1997, sold 2.81 million vehicles in 2025 and exported 1.34 million of them, up 17.4% from a year earlier. The company says it has been China's top exporter of passenger vehicles for 23 years in a row. Call for a local plant Abdi used the signing to press Chery to consider building a vehicle plant in Somalia. She pointed to the country's location on the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, its ports and its membership of the East African Community, the regional trade bloc Somalia joined in 2024. She said such an investment could create jobs and build technical skills among young Somalis. The embassy said it would keep working to expand trade and investment between Somalia and China and to help Somali companies gain access to the Chinese market. From remittances to fuel and phones Dahabshiil began in 1970 as a small trading business in Burao, in what is now Somaliland, founded by Duale's father, Mohamed Said Duale. It grew into the largest money transfer company serving the Somali diaspora and now operates in more than 120 countries, with headquarters in Dubai and more than 2,000 employees. Abdirashid Duale, who opened the company's first London branch in 1989, took over as chief executive from his father and has spread the group into banking, telecommunications, energy and real estate. Its holdings include Dahabshil Bank International, which opened in Djibouti in 2009, and a majority stake in Somali telecom operator Somtel, acquired in 2008. In 2023, the group opened the first phase of the Dahabshiil Oil Storage Terminal in the Somaliland port city of Berbera, a facility in which Dahabshiil and its partners have invested more than $100 million. somalia.content: Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday October 20, 2026 Nurto fled conflict in Baidoa and is struggling to support her seven children in Dadaab refugee camps/Ahmed Abdulahi/Ergo Families fleeing adversity in different parts of southern Somalia have been arriving in Kenya’s Dadaab refugee camps, where they find themselves with no means of making a living nor aid or support. They include families fleeing conflict in Baidoa, house demolitions by the Somali government in Mogadishu, and drought in their home areas. advertisements The new arrivals say they have received no reception support, shelter, or other forms of aid. Some are staying with relatives already struggling to make ends meet, while others have settled on their own on vacant land in Dadaab’s Ifo-2 camp. They lack food, housing, toilets and other basic services. Nurto Mohamed Ali, who arrived in Ifo-2 on 20 August, said her family had received no assistance and was struggling to meet basic needs. She is staying with relatives who arrived earlier. “Neighbours collect maize and cooking oil for us. That is how we are surviving now,” she said. “We have children who need food and bedding, but we have nothing to give them.” Nurto fled ongoing conflict in Baidoa between federal government forces and those loyal to the former South West State administration. She was a farmer raising her family on their two-hectare plot of land in Baidoa. Separated from her husband, she receives no support from him and is the sole income earner. In the refugee camp now, her seven children often go to bed hungry because she lacks food. They occupy a shelter made from plastic sheets, cloth and thorny branches in the yard of a relatives’ home – a household of 10. The days reach a scorching 37°C and the rainy season has begun. Nurto and her older children have to sleep outside without bedding while the youngest children cram themselves into the hut. Nurto said they had expected to receive assistance on arrival, including refugee registration cards, household items, and a house. She has received nothing. “We have no proper house, and even the people who arrived before us do not have one. The shelter situation is very difficult. We sleep on pieces of cloth and a small, broken mat,” she said. Other vulnerable new arrivals, including older people, people with disabilities, women and children, are finding no formal help in the camp, where some walk around daily asking more established residents for food. Hawo Mohamed Ali, her disabled husband, and their 10 children arrived in Ifo-2 on 1 August. They fled Mogadishu’s Hodan district after the government demolished their house, saying the land belonged to the state. They had lived in the house for 34 years without having formal land ownership documents. She said losing the home made it impossible for her family to remain in Mogadishu. “When we left and went outside, we found our land fenced off and surrounded by a wall,” she told Radio Ergo. “We were told the land would be measured and returned to us. Our houses were demolished using bulldozers, and we thought the land would be given back. Later, we were told it was government land and that we had to leave.” The demolition left Hawo’s family homeless and they decided their only option was to seek refuge in Dadaab. In Mogadishu, she earned a living selling meat and watermelon in local markets. In the refugee camp, however, they have not been registered and haven’t received aid cards or assistance. She looked for laundry work, but the jobs are irregular, so she has to ask others for help with food for her children. She lacks firewood and containers for collecting water. “The children’s father is disabled, and life is very difficult for us. My children are still young and have nothing here. We left our home and came to a place we do not know,” said Hawo, adding that the conditions in Dadaab were far worse than she had expected. The chairman of Hagardera camp, Khalif Dhubow Jelle, said the hardship facing new arrivals from Somalia had been brought to the attention of humanitarian agencies in the camps, but no effective response had followed. He recorded nearly 250 families having arrived from southern Somalia in the past three months. “Their living conditions are extremely poor. It is also the rainy season, yet these people have no shelter or place to stay. They are sitting in the open and have no food or water,” he said. The new arrivals are joining a refugee population already struggling with difficult living conditions because of reduced humanitarian aid and wider economic hardship across the camps. somalia.summary: Families fleeing crises in Somalia are facing dire conditions in the Dadaab refugee camps in Kenya. The camps, originally established to accommodate a temporary influx of refugees, are now home to over 200,000 people, leading to overcrowding and limited resources. Many refugees are struggling with inadequate access to food, clean water, and healthcare. The ongoing conflict, drought, and famine in Somalia have driven families to seek safety, but the camps offer little hope for a better future. Aid organizations are overwhelmed and unable to meet the growing needs of the population, leaving many refugees in a state of uncertainty and despair. The situation highlights the urgent need for international support and sustainable solutions to address the challenges faced by displaced families.

أبطال أفريقيا الهلال السوداني سيداما بونا دوري أبطال أفريقيا كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' عبر مدرب الهلال جوزيف زينباور عن سعادته بتحقيقه لفوز مهم (2-0)، على حساب مضيفه سيداما بونا الإثيوبي، اليوم الأحد 18 أكتوبر/ تشرين الأول، على ملعب "ديرا داوا" ضمن ذهاب الدور التمهيدي الثاني لمسابقة دوري أبطال أفريقيا . واعتبر مدرب النادي الأزرق أن فريقه حقق مكاسب كبيرة من خلال فوزه خارج قواعده، مهددا منافسه الإثيوبي سيداما بونا بتكرار انتصاره، مؤكدا أن فريقه لم يحسم التأهل، حيث أبدى ثقة كبيرة في بلوغ مرحلة مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا بالنظر للقوة التي أظهرها خارج ملعبه. زينباور وإشادة خاصة بحارس المرمى سفيان فريد وأكد مدرب الهلال جوزيف زينباور أن فريقه قدم مباراة متميزة لا سيما في الشوط الأول بقوله: "ترجمنا سيطرتنا على مجريات الشوط بهدف سهل من مأموريتنا، واجهنا منافسا صعبا ونجحنا في ترويضه على ملعبه". كما أشاد أيضًا بقدرات حارس المرمى سفيان فريد مؤكدا أنه قدم مباراة متميزة بقوله: "قدم فريقي مباراة متميزة، ونجح سفيان فريد في التصدي لأكثر من كرة خطيرة، أحظى بفريق جيد ونتطلع دائما للتطور". اقرأ أيضًا الهلال يضرب سيداما بونا بثنائية ويقترب من مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا كيفية مشاهدة البث المباشر لمباراة الترجي والسويحلي الليبي وشدد زينباور أن فريفه لم يضمن تأهله، مؤكدا أن جولة حاسمة تنتظره على ملعب أماهورو، قائلًا: "نسعى لتأكيد جدارتنا، ينبغي أن نحقق الفوز بجولة الحسم على ملعبنا، أثق في اللاعبين وقدرتهم على التأهل". وتابع حديثه: "علينا تقديم مستوى مماثل للذي قدمناه على ملعب منافسنا، لقد نجحنا في تقديم مستوى جيد وتحقيق فوز أعتبره مهما". وختم مدرب النادي الأزرق حديثه عن الرحلات الشاقة لفريقه، مؤكدا أن الفريق يستطيع تحقيقه هدفه المبدئي ببلوغ مرحلة مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا بقوله: "تنتظرنا رحلة شاقة أخرى، لقد أظهر نجوم الفريق صمودا وثباتا واضحا وعلينا أن نبرهن على أفضليتنا، كما ينبغي أن نحذر من منافسنا، حيث يملك الفرصة والدوافع ولكننا الأفضل والأقرب للتأهل". النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق رياضات التنس كرة السلة رياضات ميكانيكية مبارايات اليوم الأخبار football.summary: مدرب الهلال، رامون دياز، أعرب عن ثقته في قدرة فريقه على تجاوز عقبة سيداما الإثيوبي في التصفيات المؤهلة لدوري أبطال آسيا. خلال مؤتمر صحفي، أكد دياز أن الهلال يمتلك الإمكانيات اللازمة لتحقيق الفوز والتأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات. وأشار إلى أهمية المباراة وضرورة التركيز على الأداء الجيد، مشددًا على أن الفريق جاهز تمامًا لمواجهة التحديات. كما أعرب عن تفاؤله بقدرة اللاعبين على تقديم مستوى مميز يضمن لهم النجاح في هذه المرحلة الحاسمة.
